questions.question: Explain why diamond mining at Kimberley became too expensive for individual diggers.
questions.expected_answer: Claims were small, about 9.5 metres on each side, and diggers dug straight down, so the roadways between claims collapsed and ground had to be hauled up on cables. Below about 20 to 30 metres they reached hard blue ground that had to be weathered for months or crushed by machines. The surrounding reef kept falling into the pit, burying claims under rubble that cost much to remove, and water flooded the workings and had to be pumped. These problems needed steam engines, pumps and many workers. Diamond prices fell in the 1870s through overproduction and a depression hit in the late 1870s, so small diggers sold to larger holders, claim limits were relaxed in 1876 and companies formed from 1880.

questions.question: Describe how black and coloured claim owners at Kimberley lost their claims.
questions.expected_answer: In the early 1870s some Griqua, coloured and African men, including Tswana and Mfengu, held claims and employed workers. White diggers resented their competition and accused them of illicit diamond buying, though white dealers were heavily involved too. Diggers' committees demanded a ban and in July 1872 white diggers rioted, burning tents. The Southey administration did not impose an open racial ban, but rules requiring certificates of good character signed by magistrates or existing, mostly white, claim holders, strict diamond-trading rules and policing had the same effect: licences were refused or not renewed and others sold under pressure. After the Black Flag Rebellion of 1875 white diggers' interests carried more weight, and by the end of the 1870s black claim ownership had almost disappeared.

questions.question: Describe the system of labour control at Kimberley, including passes and closed compounds, and explain why the companies introduced compounds.
questions.expected_answer: African migrant workers from Pedi, Sotho, Tsonga, Tswana and eastern Cape areas worked for months and returned home. From 1872 they had to carry passes showing their employer and contract and could be arrested without one or for leaving work. Workers were searched after shifts, and IDB laws of 1880 and the Diamond Trade Act of 1882 punished illicit buying heavily. From 1885 companies introduced closed compounds: African workers lived for the length of their contracts in fenced, roofed compounds next to the mine, leaving only to work, buying goods from company stores, and were held and searched before release. White workers were not compounded. Companies said compounds prevented theft; they also controlled workers' time and wages and isolated them, and became the model for gold-mine hostels.
